profile.freedomStatement: Finishing my degree without money stress getting in the way.

profileSummary.headline: Student building calm money habits before exchange

regions.summary: See exactly where your $900 a month goes and how long your $2,500 lasts.
regions.why: You have no income right now and $900 of monthly expenses, so every dollar of your $2,500 is doing real work. Seeing that clearly is the single most useful thing you can do before anything else. It turns 'money stress' into a number you can watch.

regions.summary: Your 2-month buffer of $1,800 is already fully covered, and you carry no debt.
regions.why: Your savings cover 2.78 months of expenses, so your $1,800 emergency buffer is already met and your emergency gap is $0. With no debt either, this region is mostly about protecting what you've built rather than constructing it. The job now is keeping that buffer untouched while you study.

regions.summary: Grow the $700 you have spare beyond the buffer, mostly by finding inflow.
regions.why: Beyond your $1,800 buffer you have $700 spare, and your surplus is currently -$900 a month, so growth for you means creating inflow rather than picking anything clever. Even small, irregular income changes the shape of your year. This is where the exchange semester becomes realistic.

regions.summary: $700 of the $3,000 is already funded; $2,300 to go.
regions.why: Your exchange semester needs $3,000 and your spare savings already cover $700 of it, leaving $2,300. With no monthly surplus yet, this gap closes through new income rather than tighter spending. Naming the number makes it a plan instead of a wish.

regions.summary: Worth understanding now, worth acting on later.
regions.why: Markets can fall as well as rise over short periods, and your $700 spare is earmarked for an exchange semester rather than a long horizon, so this is a learning region for you today. Understanding it now costs nothing and removes the mystery. Relevance is 3: real, but not urgent.

regions.summary: Far off while you're studying with no income.
regions.why: Property involves deposits and ongoing costs measured in tens of thousands, which is a long way from your $2,500 and -$900 monthly surplus. Nothing here is wrong for you, it's simply years away. Relevance is 1 so it doesn't distract from your degree.

regions.summary: The most practical way for you to turn skills into inflow.
regions.why: With income at $0 a month, anything that creates cash flow matters more to you than anything that grows a balance. Small skill-based work around study hours is the realistic version of this region. Relevance is 2 because study comes first, but it's the branch most likely to move your numbers.

regions.summary: High volatility sits well outside your conservative preference.
regions.why: You've described yourself as conservative, and digital assets can move sharply in both directions over days. With money you may need for an exchange semester, that mismatch is the whole story. Relevance is 1: understand it, keep your distance for now.

regions.summary: Finishing your degree with money never being the thing that decides for you.
regions.why: You said freedom is finishing your degree without money stress getting in the way, and your buffer already covers 2.78 months, which is a real head start. This city is what it looks like when the exchange semester is funded and the buffer is still intact. Everything on the map points here.

bridges.requirement: Track one month of spending and write down your runway.
bridges.relationship: Knowing your monthly outflow is what makes a buffer meaningful
bridges.why: Your $1,800 buffer target only means something once you've confirmed $900 a month is really your outflow. Track it, and the harbour behind this bridge is already built. Skip it, and the number is just a guess.

bridges.requirement: Confirm your buffer is intact and set it aside.
bridges.relationship: Only money above the buffer is genuinely free to grow
bridges.why: Your emergency gap is $0, so the buffer part is done — the remaining work is keeping it separate from the $700 spare. Once that line is drawn you can look at growth without risking your safety net.

bridges.requirement: Create some inflow, however small or irregular.
bridges.relationship: The $2,300 gap closes with new income, not tighter spending
bridges.why: With a -$900 monthly surplus there's nothing to redirect toward the exchange semester yet. Any inflow at all is what turns $700 funded into $3,000 funded over time.

bridges.requirement: Understand how compounding works before exploring markets.
bridges.relationship: Compounding is the idea markets rest on
bridges.why: At 20, time is the biggest advantage you have, and compounding explains why. Learning it first makes everything in the markets district make sense rather than feel like noise.

bridges.requirement: Have income and savings well beyond your $1,800 buffer.
bridges.relationship: Property needs steady income before it needs anything else
bridges.why: Deposits are built from surplus, and yours is -$900 a month while you study. This bridge stays closed for now, and that's an honest reflection of where you are.

bridges.requirement: Know your runway so you can judge how much time you can give.
bridges.relationship: Your time is the capital here, and study has first call on it
bridges.why: Because your income is $0, side income is the fastest lever you have. Knowing your runway tells you how many hours a week you can spare without hurting your degree.

bridges.requirement: Complete the risk and volatility learning first.
bridges.relationship: Volatility is the entire question in this branch
bridges.why: You've said you're conservative, so this branch only makes sense after you can describe volatility in your own words. Understanding comes before anything else here.

bridges.requirement: Decide which money is for the exchange and which is long-term.
bridges.relationship: Money committed to markets is money not available for the semester
bridges.why: Your $700 spare can serve one purpose at a time, and the exchange semester has a date attached while markets need years. Naming which dollars belong to which purpose prevents an awkward decision later.

bridges.requirement: Fund the full $3,000 without touching the $1,800 buffer.
bridges.relationship: The semester funded and the buffer intact is your definition of freedom
bridges.why: You're $2,300 short today, and closing that gap while the buffer stays whole is exactly 'no money stress getting in the way'. That's what waits on the other side.

bridges.requirement: Be able to explain risk, compounding and diversification in your own words.
bridges.relationship: Understanding markets is a lifelong asset, even before any money is involved
bridges.why: You may finish your degree before you ever have long-term money to think about, and that's fine. Carrying the knowledge into that moment is worth as much as the money itself.

steps.title: See where the $900 goes
steps.description: List every outgoing for one month and group it into a handful of categories.
steps.why: You spend around $900 a month with no income coming in, so each category is a decision your past self already made. Seeing them written down is usually calmer than imagining them.

steps.title: Write down your runway
steps.description: Divide your savings by your monthly outflow and write the number of months somewhere you'll see it.
steps.why: Your $2,500 covers about 2.78 months of $900 expenses — that's your runway, and it's a fact rather than a fear. Knowing the number lets you plan around it instead of worrying about it.

steps.title: Look at the -$900 honestly
steps.description: Note what could change the monthly gap: study income, support, scholarships, term-break work.
steps.why: A surplus of -$900 isn't a failure, it's what studying with no income looks like. Listing the levers that could change it turns a scary number into a short to-do list.

steps.title: Confirm your 2-month buffer
steps.description: Check that at least $1,800 of your savings is set aside for emergencies only.
steps.why: Your emergency gap is $0 — the buffer is already there, which is genuinely uncommon at 20. This step is confirmation, not construction.

steps.title: Keep the buffer separate
steps.description: Hold the $1,800 apart from the $700 you might spend, so the two never blur.
steps.why: With no income arriving, a blurred line is how buffers quietly disappear. Keeping them separate means the exchange semester never accidentally eats your safety net.

steps.title: Create some inflow
steps.description: Identify one realistic source of money that fits around your study timetable.
steps.why: Your surplus is -$900 a month, so nothing on this map moves much until some money comes in. Even irregular inflow shortens the distance to your $2,300 gap.

steps.title: Learn how compounding works
steps.description: Understand how growth builds on previous growth over long periods.
steps.why: You're 20, which means time is the one resource you have more of than almost anyone. Understanding compounding now shapes decisions you'll make for decades.

steps.title: Size the real cost
steps.description: Break the $3,000 into its parts — fees, flights, insurance, living costs — and check nothing is missing.
steps.why: You've set $3,000 as the target and $700 is already funded, so the accuracy of that number matters. A target that's honest is one you can actually hit.

steps.title: Close the $2,300 gap
steps.description: Track the exchange fund separately and watch it move from $700 toward $3,000.
steps.why: $700 of your $3,000 is funded from spare savings, leaving $2,300 to find. Watching one number climb is far less stressful than watching a whole balance.

steps.title: Learn the language of markets
steps.description: Get clear on what shares, funds and returns actually are, without any money involved.
steps.why: Learning how markets work costs you nothing while your income is $0, and it removes a lot of the intimidation. When you do have long-term money, you'll already understand the terms.

steps.title: Test your conservative preference
steps.description: Think through how you'd feel if money set aside for years fell in value for a while.
steps.why: You've described yourself as conservative, and that's worth examining rather than assuming. Knowing your honest answer protects you from decisions that don't suit you.

steps.title: Understand what a deposit involves
steps.description: Learn how deposits, ongoing costs and timelines fit together, purely as background.
steps.why: Property is years away from $2,500 in savings and a -$900 monthly surplus, so this is context rather than a task. Understanding it early stops it feeling like a mystery later.

steps.title: List what you can offer
steps.description: Write down skills from your degree or life that someone else would pay for.
steps.why: With income at $0, your skills are the most liquid thing you own. A short honest list is often the fastest route from -$900 toward a smaller gap.

steps.title: Understand the volatility
steps.description: Learn why digital asset prices move so sharply and what that means for money with a deadline.
steps.why: Your exchange semester has a date and your buffer has a job, and neither suits large price swings. Understanding why is more useful to you than any opinion on the asset itself.

steps.title: Review your freedom statement
steps.description: Once a semester, check whether money is still getting in the way of your degree.
steps.why: Your definition of freedom is finishing your degree without money stress, so that's the only scoreboard that counts. A short honest review each semester keeps the map pointed at it.

freedomCity.title: 🕊️ City of a Clear Head
freedomCity.narrative: Your freedom is "finishing my degree without money stress getting in the way" — a $1,800 buffer that stays untouched and a $3,000 exchange semester that's fully funded. That's the whole city, and you're already partway in.

disclaimers: Free Me provides general financial education, not personal financial advice. It doesn't know your full circumstances — consider them, and seek licensed advice for decisions that matter to you.
